title: नेपाली सेनामा समावेशिता: एक विश्लेषण
nepali: आधुनिक नेपालको सबैभन्दा पुरानो संस्थाको ऐतिहासिक विरासत बोकेको नेपाली सेनाले यसको स्थापनाकाल देखि नै समावेशिताको नीतिलाई अख्तियार गरेको पाइन्छ । नेपाली सेनामा विभिन्न जातीयसमूहहरु मगर, गुरुङ, तामाङ, किराती/ लिम्बू र मधेशी समुदायहरुका बटालियनहरु नेपाली राज्यले आरक्षण कोप्रावधान सुरु गर्नुभन्दा दशकौं अघिबाट अस्तित्वमा थियो । यसले नेपाली सेनाको चरित्र स्थापना कालदेखि नै समावेशी थियो भन्ने देखाउँछ । २०७२ साल मा जारी नेपालको संविधानले आर्थिक, सामाजिक, राजनैतिक र प्रशासनिक दृष्टिले पछाडि परेका विभिन्न लक्षित वर्गहरुलाई समानुपातिक समावेशी सिद्धान्तका आधारमा राज्यको निकायमा सहभागिता हुन पाउने हकलाई मौलिक हकको रुपमा व्यवस्था गरेको छ । त्यसै अनुरुप नेपाली सेनाले पनि आफ्नो समावेशिताको मौलिक चरित्रलाई कायम राख्दै अझै समावेशी हुने तिर पाइला चालिरहेको पाइन्छ । सैनिक सेवा नियमावली, २०६९ ले खुल्ला प्रतियोगिता द्वारा नेपाली सेनामा पदपूर्ति हुने पदहरुको पैंतालिस प्रतिशत पदसंख्या समावेशीकरणका लागि छुट्याई सो संख्यालाई शत प्रतिशत मानी महिला, आदिवासी/जनजाति, मधेशी, दलित र पिछडिएको क्षेत्रका उम्मेदवारहरु बिचक्रमश: बिस, बत्तिस, अट्ठाइस, पन्ध्र र पॉच प्रतिशत छुट्याएर ती समूह/समुदायका उम्मेदवारहरु बिच मात्र प्रतिस्पर्धा गर्ने प्रावधान लागू गरी नेपाली सेनामा पनि आरक्षण मार्फत् प्रतिनिधित्व बढाउने प्रयास गरिएकोछ । २०६२/०६३ को राजनैतिक परिवर्तनपछि राज्यका अन्य अङ्गहरुमा झै नेपाली सेनामा पनि समावेशी गर्नुपर्ने प्रावधानहरुले गति पायो । समावेशीकरणको नीति नेपाली राज्यका अन्य अङ्गहरु झैं नेपाली सेनाले पनि अङ्गीकार गर्दा त्यसका राम्रा र नराम्रा असरहरु नेपाली सेनाले पनि भोगिरहेको छ । द्धितीयक स्रोतका तथ्याकंहरुको विश्लेषणका आधारमा नेपाली सेनामा समावेशिताको विगतदेखि हालसम्मको अवस्था विश्लेषण गर्दे आगामी दिनमा पनि नेपाली सेनालेआफ्नो समावेशी चरित्र मार्फत् नेपाल राष्ट्र/राज्यको सार्वभौमसत्ता, अखण्डतालाई कसरी जोगाई राख्न सक्छ भन्ने विश्लेषण यो लेखमा समेटिएको छ ।
american_english: Carrying the historical legacy of modern Nepal's oldest institution, the Nepali Army is found to have adopted a policy of inclusivity from the very time of its establishment. In the Nepali Army, battalions of various ethnic groups—Magar, Gurung, Tamang, Kirati/Limbu, and Madhesi communities—existed decades before the Nepali state initiated the provision of reservations. This demonstrates that the character of the Nepali Army was inclusive right from its founding era. The Constitution of Nepal promulgated in 2072 BS has provided as a fundamental right the right of various target classes, left behind economically, socially, politically, and administratively, to participate in state bodies on the basis of proportional inclusive principles. In line with that, the Nepali Army too is found to be taking steps toward becoming even more inclusive while maintaining the original character of its inclusivity. The Military Service Rules, 2069 allocated forty-five percent of posts to be filled through open competition in the Nepali Army for inclusion, and regarding that number as one hundred percent, allocated twenty, thirty-two, twenty-eight, fifteen, and five percent respectively among candidates of women, indigenous nationalities/Janajati, Madhesi, Dalit, and backward areas, implementing a provision to compete only among candidates of those groups/communities, thereby making an effort to increase representation through reservations in the Nepali Army as well. Following the political change of 2062/063 BS, provisions requiring inclusion gathered momentum in the Nepali Army just as in other organs of the state. As the Nepali Army adopted the policy of inclusion just as other organs of the Nepali state did, it too has been experiencing its positive and negative effects. Based on the analysis of data from secondary sources, while analyzing the status of inclusivity in the Nepali Army from past to present, this article incorporates an analysis of how the Nepali Army can preserve the sovereignty and integrity of the Nepal nation/state through its inclusive character in the days ahead as well.

informal_english: Carrying the historical legacy of modern Nepal's oldest institution, the Nepali Army has pretty much backed a policy of inclusion right from the start. In the Nepali Army, battalions from different ethnic groups—Magar, Gurung, Tamang, Kirati/Limbu, and Madhesi communities—were already around decades before the Nepali state ever brought in reservation quotas. That really shows the character of the Nepali Army was inclusive right from the get-go. The Constitution of Nepal brought in back in 2072 BS set up the right for different targeted groups left behind economically, socially, politically, and administratively to take part in state bodies under proportional inclusion as a fundamental right. Following on from that, the Nepali Army has also been taking steps towards getting even more inclusive while keeping its original inclusive character intact. The Military Service Rules, 2069 set aside forty-five percent of posts filled by open competition in the Nepali Army for inclusion, counted that share as one hundred percent, and split it twenty, thirty-two, twenty-eight, fifteen, and five percent respectively between candidates of women, indigenous nationalities/Janajati, Madhesi, Dalit, and backward regions, making it so candidates only compete within those groups, which was an effort to boost representation in the army through quotas as well. After the political change in 2062/063 BS, provisions to make things inclusive really gathered pace in the Nepali Army just like in other organs of the state. With the Nepali Army taking on board the policy of inclusion just like other state bodies did, it's also been experiencing both the good and bad fallout from it. Looking at data from secondary sources to check out how inclusive the Nepali Army has been from past to present, this article covers an analysis of how the army can keep safeguarding the sovereignty and integrity of the Nepal nation-state through its inclusive character in the days ahead as well.
